account1_proposal.proposed_short: At a Sept. 22, 2017 Huntsville rally, Trump urged NFL owners to fire kneeling players and used the phrase “son of a bitch.”
account1_proposal.proposed_medium: At a September 22, 2017, rally in Huntsville, Alabama, Trump urged NFL owners to remove players who knelt during the national anthem, using the phrase “Get that son of a bitch off the field” and saying “He’s fired.” The transcript supports the insult and call for dismissal; it does not describe physical violence.
account1_proposal.proposed_long: The official transcript of Donald Trump’s September 22, 2017, campaign rally for Senator Luther Strange in Huntsville, Alabama, records remarks about NFL players who knelt during the national anthem. Trump asked whether owners should say, “Get that son of a bitch off the field right now,” and added, “He’s fired. He’s fired!” He also urged offended fans to leave stadiums. The transcript directly supports reporting the insult and his call for owners to dismiss protesting players. The event should be described as a political rally statement, not as physical violence or a specific threat of bodily harm. The quoted remarks do not substantiate claims about what teams subsequently did or how every player protest was treated. The record identifies this as a campaign rally for Senator Luther J. Strange III. It is not a report of NFL discipline or league action; it records Trump’s proposed response and his suggested fan response that night.

proposed_fields.description_long: Robert I. Friedman’s Red Mafiya was published in 2000. The reviewer characterizes the book as an exposé but cautions that it has no notes, making some of Friedman’s dramatic findings difficult to verify, and says some accusations might not stand in a criminal case. The linked New York Times archive is a separate report about money laundering in Israel and the Bank of New York investigation; it does not quote Friedman. The TrumpFile entry itself says the exact quotation was pending and identifies no connection to Donald Trump. This draft summarizes the book’s documented subject and review, while recommending exclusion from a Trump-specific chronology unless a Trump nexus is sourced.

According to advisers quoted by the newspaper, Tim Parlatore, Pete Hegseth’s personal lawyer and a supervisor of the inquiry, suggested investigators had found a warrantless wiretap on an aide’s phone. The report says Parlatore later denied that a wiretap had occurred and that White House advisers regarded the claim as untrue. The Guardian also reported that the inquiry moved to Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg’s office around the time Parlatore planned to step away. These accounts support a headline about conflicting reports and the handling of the investigation. They do not establish that Hegseth or Parlatore knowingly lied, which would require evidence about what each person knew when speaking. The corrected description attributes each assertion to the reporting and does not turn a disputed account into a finding of intentional deception.

account1_proposal.proposed_title: Trump Pardoned More Than 1,000 January 6 Defendants and Commuted 14 Sentences
account1_proposal.proposed_description_short: On January 20, 2025, Trump pardoned more than 1,000 people tied to January 6 and commuted 14 sentences, CNN reported.
account1_proposal.proposed_description_medium: CNN reported that Trump’s January 20, 2025 clemency actions included pardons for more than 1,000 people charged in connection with the January 6 attack and commutations for 14 others. NPR described roughly 1,500 pardons. These reports do not support an 1,840-plus total across all clemency actions or a transactional motive.
account1_proposal.proposed_description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued broad clemency for people charged in connection with the January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol. CNN reported that he pardoned more than 1,000 people and commuted the sentences of 14 others; NPR’s contemporaneous account described pardons for roughly 1,500 defendants. CNN noted that some people whose sentences were commuted were associated with the Proud Boys and Oath Keepers and explained that a commutation reduces or ends a sentence without being the same legal action as a pardon. These sources support the scale and date of the January 6 clemency actions, but not a single 1,840-plus aggregate spanning unrelated pardons or other clemency. They also do not establish that the actions were exchanged for money or political support. The corrected title uses the supported “more than 1,000” count and distinguishes pardons from commutations. Any claims about corruption pardons, a broader aggregate total or transactional motive require separate case-specific evidence and should not be attached to this event.

source_to_fact_mapping.supports: Sections 70512 and 70513 amend the clean-electricity production credit under IRC §45Y and investment credit under §48E, including the covered wind/solar termination rules and transition provisions; the act was signed July 4, 2025.

source_to_fact_mapping.publisher: U.S. House Office of the Law Revision Counsel
source_to_fact_mapping.supports: Current 26 U.S.C. §45Y contains the December 31, 2027 cutoff for covered facilities, subject to statutory terms.
source_to_fact_mapping.access_note: Official codification for §45Y; the enacted law remains the source for the related §48E amendment.

unsupported_or_rejected_claims: The statute did not repeal every IRA clean-energy credit and does not establish blanket clawback of already committed funds across solar, wind, batteries, and EV manufacturing. Reuters’ broad investment coverage is not used to prove legal scope.
account1_proposal.uncertainty: The proposed description concerns defined facilities and two credit sections only. Project eligibility depends on statutory definitions, construction timing, and transition provisions; this row makes no claim about every project or credit.

independent_qa.exact_reason: Public Law 119-21 supports the July 4, 2025 enactment and wind/solar cutoffs after December 31, 2027, but the proposed phrase “subject to statutory transition rules” blurs distinct §45Y and §48E rules and omits §48E’s express energy-storage exception. The U.S. Code URL was under maintenance; Congress.gov primary law is accessible.
independent_qa.claim_scope_review: The date and high-level statement are correct, but “covered wind and solar facilities ... subject to statutory transition rules” is too vague to represent the differing statute provisions, especially the storage exception in §48E. Do not imply that all credits or all facility property terminate.
independent_qa.recommended_correction: Revise to identify covered §45Y facilities and §48E qualified property at applicable facilities separately, including the §48E energy-storage exception; cite the enacted law.

source_reviews.supports: Public Law 119-21 §§70512–70513 amend IRC §§45Y and 48E; the text sets the December 31, 2027 placed-in-service cutoff for applicable wind/solar facilities/property and gives §48E an express exception for energy storage technology at an applicable facility.
source_reviews.limits: Avoid implying blanket termination of every project/property at a wind/solar site; distinguish the §45Y and §48E language and their exceptions. “Transition rules” is not an adequate substitute for the actual scope.

account1_proposal.corrected_title: Yujing Zhang Sentenced After Trespassing at Mar-a-Lago
account1_proposal.corrected_short: Yujing Zhang was convicted of entering a restricted area at Mar-a-Lago and making false statements to a federal officer; she was sentenced to eight months.
account1_proposal.corrected_medium: In March 2019, Secret Service agents arrested Yujing Zhang after she entered a restricted area at Mar-a-Lago. CNN reported that she was convicted of unlawfully entering a restricted area and making false statements to a federal officer, then sentenced to eight months in prison in November. This case does not establish routine foreign access to the president or access to classified meetings.
account1_proposal.corrected_long: In March 2019, Secret Service agents arrested Yujing Zhang after she entered a restricted area at Mar-a-Lago. In November, a federal jury found her guilty of unlawfully entering a restricted area and making false statements to a federal officer, and a judge sentenced her to eight months in prison, according to CNN. This is a specific visitor-screening and criminal case. It does not establish that foreign nationals routinely had access to the president during either of his terms, that Zhang reached classified meetings, or that the club lacked secure communications for every presidential activity. The account also avoids repeating the claim that a thumb drive proved an espionage operation: contemporary reporting described an initial malware test as potentially a false positive, and the reviewed source does not establish that malware was used. The broader claims about a foreign-intelligence “honeypot,” persistent counterintelligence failure, and access by Russian or other foreign nationals require independent reporting or records. The revised entry is limited to Zhang’s entry, conviction, and sentence, with the limits of this single case made explicit.
